source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? A Large-Scale Human Study with 100+ NLP Researchers
finding: Blind expert review of ideas on 7 NLP topics. LLM-agent ideas were rated more novel than ideas written by experts, with feasibility slightly lower.
numbers: 49 ideas per condition (Human, AI, AI+human rerank). 79 reviewers, 298 reviews, 49 writers. Novelty per review: Human 4.84 (N=119), AI 5.64 (N=109, p=0.00**), AI+Rerank 5.81 (p=0.00***). Feasibility: Human 6.61, AI 6.34, Rerank 6.44 (none significant). Per-idea averages: novelty AI 5.62 (p=0.03), Rerank 5.78 (p=0.00).
limits: Only 7 NLP prompting topics; ideas not executed; reviews subjective.
agent_relevance: Shows a model can propose questions that look novel to experts. Novelty at the S0 gate cannot be trusted without execution (see a05).

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? A Large-Scale Human Study with 100+ NLP Researchers
finding: Reviewer agreement on research ideas is low: 56.1% for ideas, below the 66.0% found in the NeurIPS 2021 consistency experiment for papers.
numbers: Agreement 56.1% (this study) vs 66.0% (NeurIPS 2021).
limits: Authors treat idea review as even more subjective than paper review.
agent_relevance: Ground truth about which question is good is noisy even for experts. A selector should not expect clean labels.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? A Large-Scale Human Study with 100+ NLP Researchers
finding: LLM idea generation does not scale in diversity. Of 4000 seed ideas per topic, about 5% survive deduplication; unique ideas plateau near 200 per topic.
numbers: 4000 seeds per topic; cosine similarity threshold 0.8 (all-MiniLM-L6-v2); about 5% non-duplicate; about 200 unique per topic. Ranker accuracy on ICLR review pairs: Claude-3.5-Sonnet 71.4%, Claude-3-Opus 63.5%, GPT-4o 61.1%.
limits: Embedding dedup is crude. Single model family.
agent_relevance: Over-generate then select saturates fast. More samples add few new questions. Diversity needs different seeds or retrieval, not more draws.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? A Large-Scale Human Study with 100+ NLP Researchers
finding: Design control: an LLM style-normalizer rewrote all ideas into one format so reviewers could not tell the source. Experts distinguished AI from human ideas at chance. Human reranking of the AI pool differed much from the LLM ranker.
numbers: Expert accuracy at telling AI from human after normalization: 50% (small study). Only 17 of the 49 AI+Rerank ideas overlap with the 49 LLM-ranker picks; 32 differ.
limits: Small check of the normalizer.
agent_relevance: Supports G8: the model's own ranking of ideas disagrees with an expert's. Do not let the generator choose the question.

source: Si, Hashimoto, Yang (2025) The Ideation-Execution Gap: Execution Outcomes of LLM-Generated versus Human Research Ideas
finding: When 43 experts spent over 100 hours each executing randomly assigned ideas, the LLM ideas lost their novelty advantage. AI ideas dropped much more in score after execution than human ideas.
numbers: N=19 human-idea and N=24 AI-idea projects, 58 reviewers. Ideation novelty/excitement/effectiveness/overall: Human 4.91/4.40/4.83/4.60, AI 5.78/5.65/6.00/5.38 (FDR p 0.035/0.004/0.001/0.035). After execution: Human 4.90/4.48/4.78/3.97, AI 4.73/3.90/4.13/3.41 (no significant difference). Gaps: Human -0.010/+0.078/-0.052/-0.628; AI -1.049/-1.760/-1.879/-1.976 (p 0.025/0.001/0.003/0.004).
limits: Small N (43 projects), one NLP domain, executors changed some ideas (explains only a small part of the gap).
agent_relevance: Strongest evidence that ideation-time judgement of a question is biased toward LLM text. The S0 gate should test cheaply by running, not by rating.

source: Si, Hashimoto, Yang (2025) The Ideation-Execution Gap: Execution Outcomes of LLM-Generated versus Human Research Ideas
finding: Ideation scores weakly predicted execution scores. For AI ideas there was even a moderately negative correlation on excitement.
numbers: Correlation between ideation and execution scores: weak in most metrics (Appendix D); moderately negative for AI-idea excitement.
limits: Small N, wide intervals.
agent_relevance: Pre-run rating of a question has little predictive value, so a cheap probe run is worth more than a rating step.

source: Wen et al. (2025) Predicting Empirical AI Research Outcomes with Language Models
finding: Task: given two research ideas, predict which scores better on benchmarks. Off-the-shelf frontier models are near chance; a fine-tuned GPT-4.1 with paper retrieval reaches 77% on the full test set.
numbers: 1,585 human-verified idea pairs for test (after base model cutoff), 6,000 for training. Zero-shot GPT-4.1 51.9%; o1 and o3 similar or slightly better. Fine-tuned system 77%. On unpublished ideas including AI-agent ideas: 63.6%.
limits: Pairs come from published papers (survivorship). Narrow domain: empirical AI benchmarks.
agent_relevance: A learned outcome predictor can choose between questions, but only with training on past outcomes. A prompted model alone has no taste. Possible reward model for S0 in a domain with logged results.

source: Wen et al. (2025) Predicting Empirical AI Research Outcomes with Language Models
finding: Experts did worse than the system. Majority vote of 5 NLP experts got 48.9% on 45 pairs, even though they agreed with each other 75.1% of the time.
numbers: 25 experts, 222 valid labels on 45 pairs. Majority vote 48.9%. Best-per-topic ceiling baseline 60.0%. System on same subset 64.4%. Inter-annotator agreement 75.1% vs NeurIPS 2021 reviewer agreement 75.8%.
limits: Small N (45 pairs).
agent_relevance: Agreement among judges is not evidence of being right (supports G4).

source: Wen et al. (2025) Predicting Empirical AI Research Outcomes with Language Models
finding: Pipeline detail matters: summarising whole papers instead of abstracts lifts accuracy, because abstracts bias the model toward old ideas.
numbers: Retrieval-augmented accuracy 38.8% with abstracts to 53.0% with full-paper summaries (Table 3).
limits: Single system.
agent_relevance: When the agent checks prior work for a candidate question, read more than abstracts.

source: Gupta & Pruthi (2025) All That Glitters is Not Novel: Plagiarism in AI Generated Research
finding: Experts told to search for overlap found that many LLM research proposals copy existing work: 24% paraphrased or heavily borrowed, cross-verified by source authors.
numbers: 50 LLM proposals, 13 experts. 24.0% verified plagiarism (36.0% if unverified claims counted). Only a small fraction judged completely novel.
limits: 50 proposals; convenience sample of experts; includes proposals from the Si 2024 release.
agent_relevance: Novelty claims for generated questions must be checked by retrieval against the literature.

source: Gupta & Pruthi (2025) All That Glitters is Not Novel: Plagiarism in AI Generated Research
finding: Automated plagiarism checkers fail on rewritten ideas. Retrieval of the source paper is the bottleneck.
numbers: Turnitin and OpenScholar found the source in 0 cases (36 tested). Oracle-access LLM check 88.8% (Claude 3.5 Sonnet) and 89.0% (GPT-4o); parametric knowledge only 1.3% and 32.7%; SSAG pipeline 51.3% and 68.5%.
limits: Small tests (3 papers per topic).
agent_relevance: The novelty check must use retrieval, not the model's memory, and its recall is the weak part.

source: Wang et al. (2023) SciMON: Scientific Inspiration Machines Optimized for Novelty
finding: Idea generation from a background context with retrieved inspirations, then iterative rewriting against retrieved prior work to raise novelty. Outputs stay below the original papers.
numbers: Against ground-truth ideas, the true paper idea had higher technical level and novelty in 85% of comparisons. Iterative boosting made 54.4% of first-iteration ideas more novel and 57.8% in a second iteration (variant). Extraction pipeline passed 79.7% of instances.
limits: Small human evaluation; novelty compared with the original paper's idea.
agent_relevance: A novelty loop against retrieved prior work is a workable mechanism; generated output is still below real papers.

source: Baek et al. (2024) ResearchAgent: Iterative Research Idea Generation over Scientific Literature with LLMs
finding: Agent builds problem, method and experiment design from a core paper plus an entity knowledge graph, then refines with reviewer agents whose criteria are induced from human judgements. Scores rise over refinement steps.
numbers: Scores on a 1 to 5 scale rise across refinement steps; final scores around 4 to 4.5 in reported figures (exact values not extracted).
limits: Judged mostly by LLM reviewing agents calibrated on few human pairs; self-judging risk.
agent_relevance: Typical self-judged loop. Weaker evidence than the blind human studies in a01 to a07.

source: Lu et al. (2024) The AI Scientist: Towards Fully Automated Open-Ended Scientific Discovery
finding: AI Scientist generates about 50 ideas per template, filters them by a Semantic Scholar novelty check done by the model itself, then runs experiments. Most ideas pass the novelty flag; fewer finish.
numbers: Diffusion template, 51 ideas each: Sonnet 3.5 49 novel, 38 experiments passed, 38 papers, mean automated review score 3.82 (max 6.0), $250; GPT-4o 41/17/16, 3.70, $300; DeepSeek Coder 42/32/31, 3.32, $10; Llama-3.1 405B 31/21/21, 2.30, $120.
limits: Paper says novelty check is self-assessed by each model, so cross-model comparison is unreliable. Reviewer is an LLM.
agent_relevance: Problem selection by generate plus self-checked novelty. The audit in a10 and a11 shows this lets through copied ideas.

source: Krenn & Zeilinger (2020) Predicting research trends with semantic and neural networks (SEMNET)
finding: Formal model of which question comes next: a network of 6,368 quantum physics concepts built from 750,000 papers; an MLP over 17 network properties predicts which unlinked concept pairs will be studied together within 5 years.
numbers: Papers since 1919. About 5% of all possible edges drawn by end of 2017. ROC AUC for 5-year link prediction 0.85 (2017 data, trained on 2012 and earlier); 1995 and 2005 tests also above random 0.5. Pairs sharing under 20% of neighbors only.
limits: Quantum physics only; concepts from Wikipedia and manual lists; co-occurrence, not meaning.
agent_relevance: Problem choice is partly predictable from graph structure. Predicted likely-next is not the same as valuable (see a16).

source: Gu & Krenn (v4, 2026) Generating Interesting Scientific Ideas using Knowledge Graphs and LLMs: Evaluations with 100 Research Group Leaders (SciMuse)
finding: Expert rating of personalized LLM ideas for interest was modest, and graph-chosen concept pairs did not beat a titles-only GPT baseline.
numbers: More than 4,400 ideas rated by 100+ group leaders; mean 2.40 of 5, most common rating 1, 24.9% rated 4 or 5. Graph of 58 million papers. 267 invited, 110 took part (41.2%). Predicted high-citation pairs had a weak tendency toward lower interest (1.94) than random pairs. 2,996 graph-based suggestions analysed.
limits: Self-selected raters; personalized ideas.
agent_relevance: Predicted impact of a concept pair did not turn into expert interest. A supervised graph-feature network and a zero-shot LLM ranker can predict interest, so a ranker in S0 is possible but needs calibration data.

source: Sourati & Evans (2023) Accelerating science with human-aware artificial intelligence
finding: Model of problem choice that includes scientists: a hypergraph of papers, materials, properties and authors, random walks and DeepWalk embeddings. Predicting what humans will study next lifts forecasts of discoveries; the model can also be tuned to avoid the crowd.
numbers: Up to 400% better prediction than content-only models, especially for sparse literature. About 100% average precision gain for materials properties (1.5M inorganic materials articles, 1937 to 2018). 43% higher precision for drug-disease associations at 18 years. COVID-19 drug candidates entering trials: 36-38% rising to 42% vs 10-12% content-only. 40% of top-50 predicted authors became discoverers one year later for thermoelectric and ferroelectric materials.
limits: Retrospective on materials and biomedicine; a sampling parameter sets crowd-following vs crowd-avoiding.
agent_relevance: Gives a formal tool: the question experts will soon ask is predictable, and the question they would not reach can be sampled on purpose. Open mode could sample both ends.

source: Foster, Rzhetsky, Evans (2015) Tradition and Innovation in Scientists' Research Strategies, American Sociological Review
finding: Typology of research strategies on chemical networks from MEDLINE abstracts: innovation (new chemicals or relations) vs tradition (known ones); consolidating vs bridging. High-risk innovation is rare and the mix is stable. Innovative papers get more impact, but not enough to pay for the risk of not publishing.
numbers: Abstract only, read through Crossref; no numbers captured. Abstract: millions of MEDLINE abstracts; prizewinner gambles explain the observed level of risky innovation.
limits: Not opened in full (publisher returned 403). Numbers must be added by a later pass.
agent_relevance: Core theory: the essential tension between productive tradition and risky innovation, with Bourdieu's field logic. S0 can model a deliberate tradition/innovation mix.

source: Rzhetsky, Foster, Foster, Evans (2015) Choosing experiments to accelerate collective discovery, PNAS
finding: Network model of knowledge plus a sequence of experiments. Over 30 years of MEDLINE articles, scientists follow conservative strategies near central, well-known molecules. This slows collective discovery, especially in mature fields.
numbers: Abstract only via Crossref: millions of biomedical articles over 30 years; no figures captured.
limits: Not opened in full (PNAS and PMC blocked). Simulation numbers not captured.
agent_relevance: Problem selection as search on a network; conservative choice is individually rational but collectively slow. A single agent has no career incentive and could explore more.

source: Fortunato et al. (2018) Science of science, Science 359(6379)
finding: Review that frames science of science as a large-data study of the mechanisms of science, from the choice of a research problem to careers and progress.
numbers: Abstract only via Crossref.
limits: Not opened in full (publisher 403).
agent_relevance: Map of the subfield; no numbers used.

source: Gross & Bergstrom (2019) Contest models highlight inefficiencies of scientific funding, PLOS Biology
finding: Contest model: when awards are fewer than meritorious proposals, effort spent on proposals can equal the value of the funded work. Funding structure steers what gets proposed.
numbers: Cost c(v,x)=x^2/v, one third recouped as intellectual value; project values 0.25 to 1; paylines 45% and 15% compared. Survey cited: faculty spend 8% of total time and 19% of research time on proposals. Partial lotteries avoid the loss.
limits: Illustrative parameters, not calibrated; qualitative. Read via a WebFetch summary, not the raw PDF.
agent_relevance: Incentives shape which questions are chosen. An agent with a fixed budget should split it between probing and executing (G12).

source: Kuhn (1959) The Essential Tension; Kitcher (1990) The division of cognitive labor
finding: Background only. Kuhn's essential tension between convergent tradition and divergent innovation is the stated source for Foster et al. Kitcher argued a community does better when scientists spread across approaches than when all choose the best-looking one.
numbers: None captured this session.
limits: Not opened; stated from memory. Do not use numbers.
agent_relevance: A portfolio of questions beats always taking the top-ranked one; but G4 says samples from one model are not independent, so a portfolio needs real diversity.

source: Gupta & Pruthi (2025) All That Glitters is Not Novel
finding: Case study: the proposal 'Semantic Resonance Uncertainty Quantification', an exemplar released with Si 2024, maps one to one onto an existing paper (Lin et al. 2023) with reworded terms. The original authors confirmed it.
numbers: One proposal; similarity score 5 of 5; terms renamed (e.g. resonance graph for weighted adjacency matrix).
limits: Single case.
agent_relevance: An idea rated novel by blind experts in a01 can still be a rewrite. Rewrites defeat embedding and text-match checks.

source: Gu & Krenn (2026) SciMuse
finding: Interest in AI-generated ideas varies sharply by person and the average is low; only about a quarter are rated good, so selection among many candidates matters more than the first draft.
numbers: Mean 2.40 of 5; 24.9% rated 4 or 5; 394 suggestions got a 5.
limits: Raters judged ideas for their own field.
agent_relevance: Expect most generated questions to be poor; budget for filtering rather than for polishing a single draft.

source: Lu et al. (2024) The AI Scientist
finding: The authors list limits: the automated reviewer data (ICLR 2022) may be in model training data, and Llama 3.1 405B struggled to follow the reviewer output format; GPT-4o often failed to write LaTeX, which blocked completion.
numbers: Completed papers: GPT-4o 16 of 51; Sonnet 3.5 38 of 51.
limits: Self-reported limitations section.
agent_relevance: Execution failure is common, so a probe run in the S0 gate should be cheap and tolerate failure.
